title: Why I’m becoming a China bear
gist: Former China bull Noah Smith turns bearish: Xi's subsidy-driven 'make-everything country' strategy is hitting limits (shrinking manufacturing share, export-market saturation, collapsing sector profits, infrastructure leveling off, property bust), Xi's politics are deteriorating, and AI will upend the production era China is optimized for — making him a China dove; the AI section is truncated by a paywall.

themes.theme: Smith's regime change: from China bull/hawk to bear/dove

insights.claim: Noah Smith, long a China bull who expected a 'Chinese Century', now says he is becoming bearish for the first time: China will stay immensely powerful but US-style global hegemony is likely out of reach and its bid for tech dominance is weaker than he believed.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A prominent former China bull turning bearish signals a shift in consensus on China's long-run growth and power.
insights.quote: I’m starting to think that global hegemony of the type the U.S. enjoyed throughout most of the 20th century will be out of reach
insights.locator: Now, however, for the first time

insights.claim: Smith says his growing bearishness makes him more of a China dove: friend-shoring, export controls and military alliances are still prudent but now feel like an insurance policy rather than a desperate urgency.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Reduced hawkish urgency among analysts could soften pressure for escalating US-China decoupling measures.
insights.quote: they feel more like an insurance policy now
insights.locator: And just as my previous bullishness

insights.claim: Smith gives three reasons for downgrading China: AI (the biggest, since China's system is optimized for a production era ending quickly), the likely failure of its push to capture global high-tech manufacturing, and deteriorating politics under Xi Jinping's spiraling paranoia.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: AI disruption is framed as the main threat to China's growth model — relevant for long China/EM allocation.
insights.quote: China’s system is incredibly optimized for an era of technology and economic production that is very quickly coming to an end.

insights.claim: Smith never saw demographic decline as a major threat to China's power, and expects population decline to shrink the domestic market meaningfully only from around 2040.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Demographics are a slow-moving drag; near-term China risks are elsewhere.
insights.quote: I don’t expect this to be a big factor until at least 2040 or so
insights.locator: And of course as the years go by

insights.claim: Xi Jinping's strategy is to make China the 'make-everything country', resisting the normal shift to services as countries get rich and spending about 4% of GDP a year subsidizing manufacturing, mostly through cheap bank loans.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Massive subsidy-driven capacity underlies global overcapacity and deflationary pressure in traded goods.
insights.quote: spending about 4% of GDP per year on subsidizing manufacturing industries
insights.locator: In order to make China dominate global manufacturing

insights.claim: China increasingly uses export controls on items from tunnel-boring machines to rare earths, drones and medicines as bludgeons to force other nations to do its bidding.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Supply-chain coercion risk for rare earths, drones and pharma inputs remains a key geopolitical exposure.
insights.quote: using export controls on everything from tunnel-boring machines to rare earths to drones to medicines as bludgeons

insights.claim: A 2024 UNIDO paper projected China's share of global manufacturing would reach 45% by 2030, but more reasonable projections put it at about 35-36% as share growth has slowed; in US dollar terms China's share peaked during the pandemic and has drifted down.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: China's manufacturing share expansion is plateauing, tempering 'Second China Shock' fears.
insights.quote: more reasonable predictions put its 2030 share at maybe 35-36%
insights.locator: For a while, this seemed to be working

insights.claim: Despite Xi's push, manufacturing is a shrinking share of China's economy, and China is now less industrial than South Korea despite being less than half as rich.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Policy is fighting structural forces; watch manufacturing share of GDP as a test of Xi's strategy.
insights.quote: China is now less industrial than South Korea, despite being less than half as rich

insights.claim: Because China is so large, the gravity model of trade means export markets will saturate, so its manufacturers must rely on the domestic market; China cannot be a 'Giant Korea' and remains far less export-intensive than Korea.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Export-led growth has a ceiling for China, putting the burden on weak domestic demand.
insights.quote: China simply can’t be Giant Korea

insights.claim: The EU recently forced China into a deal to limit auto imports, and Smith expects stronger measures if it fails, accelerating saturation of China's export markets.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Rising trade barriers on Chinese autos and EVs; watch EU follow-on measures.
insights.quote: The EU recently forced China to make a deal to limit auto imports
insights.locator: Of course, some countries will put tariffs

insights.claim: Profits in China's auto, steel, solar and other manufacturing sectors are collapsing as weak demand from the real estate bust meets subsidy-driven oversupply, which Smith expects to force closures and consolidation and starve private firms of R&D budgets.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Bearish for Chinese industrial earnings; expect consolidation and continued export price pressure.
insights.quote: Profits in the auto sector, the steel sector, the solar sector, and many other manufacturing industries are all collapsing.
insights.locator: China simply can’t be Giant Korea

insights.claim: Chinese manufacturing indicators are faltering and manufacturing investment appears to have topped out, suggesting subsidies have reached their limit.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Peak manufacturing investment implies slowing capex demand for commodities and machinery.
insights.quote: manufacturing investment seems to have topped out as well
insights.locator: Government subsidies can keep the party

insights.claim: Smith argues China's manufacturing gains depended on the tailwind of the long property boom, so Xi cannot shift resources one-for-one from real estate into manufacturing, and weak demand will make it hard to hold even 30% global share.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Property weakness is a direct headwind to Chinese manufacturing market share, not just to GDP.
insights.quote: demand matters, and China’s manufacturing triumphs in past decades depended heavily on the tailwind that the long property boom had been delivering
insights.locator: Weak domestic demand won’t just be a drag

insights.claim: China's infrastructure investment has leveled off; a senior transport official said the main transport network was '91% complete' and China would pivot from expanding to upgrading.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: End of China's infrastructure splurge reduces demand for steel, cement and construction commodities.
insights.quote: China’s main transport network was “91% complete”
insights.locator: In fact, this isn’t even the only example

insights.claim: Smith argues China's infrastructure overbuild locks it into spending a significant fraction of GDP maintaining underused roads, rail and bridges due to depreciation, unless it lets some decay.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Maintenance burdens crowd out productive investment and weigh on growth and local-government finances.
insights.quote: That’s the iron logic of depreciation.
insights.locator: But it isn’t so easy weaning yourself

insights.claim: Smith expects China's growth to slow amid the protracted real estate bust, with signs the real economic damage in that sector is only getting started.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Bearish signal for China growth-sensitive assets and commodity demand.
insights.quote: There are signs that the real economic damage in that sector is only getting started
insights.locator: All of this means growth will slow.

themes.theme: Xi's governance and the AI threat

insights.claim: Smith argues Xi Jinping has stopped listening to economists and purged officials inclined to listen, illustrating the weaknesses of authoritarian systems as his paranoia turns China inward.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Policy-making risk is rising; don't assume Beijing will course-correct quickly on demand stimulus.
insights.quote: Xi seems to have stopped listening to economists, and to have purged his government of anyone who was inclined to listen
insights.locator: Xi seems to think that China

insights.claim: Smith predicts the failure of the manufacturing strategy will coincide with an AI revolution that China is not well prepared to exploit, and that China will probably flub the Age of AI (argument truncated by paywall).
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Contrarian to the narrative of Chinese AI parity; implies relative advantage for US AI leaders.
insights.quote: a revolution that China, despite all reports, is not well-prepared to take advantage of
